metadata.title: How it works
metadata.description: Learn how Blind Journal encrypts journal content in your browser, separates authentication from decryption, and stores only protected records on the server.

hero.title: How Blind Journal protects your writing
hero.body: Blind Journal is designed so your journal can be stored remotely without giving the server the keys needed to read it. This page walks through where encryption happens, how sign-in works, what gets stored, and what the server can and cannot see.

bigPicture.title: Where does my journal get encrypted?
bigPicture.body: Your journal is encrypted in your browser before it is sent to Blind Journal’s server. The readable version stays on your side of that boundary, while the server receives encrypted journal data instead.
bigPicture.httpsBody: HTTPS protects the connection between your browser and the server, but it does not hide data from the server itself. Blind Journal encrypts your journal before it crosses that connection, so HTTPS carries encrypted journal data rather than the readable entry.

authentication.title: How can the server sign me in without being able to read my journal?
authentication.body: When you enter your passphrase, Blind Journal processes it in your browser and derives separate key material for different purposes. One branch is used to authenticate with the server. Another stays in the browser and is used to unlock the keys that protect your journal.
authentication.separationBody: The server receives the authentication key it needs to verify your sign-in, but not your passphrase or the key-encryption material that unlocks journal entry keys. Because those purposes are derived separately, the authentication key cannot be used to decrypt journal content.

saving.title: What happens when I press Save?
saving.body: When you press Save, the browser creates a fresh random key for that entry and uses it to encrypt the title and body before anything is sent.
saving.storageBody: That entry key is then protected with key-encryption material that remains in the browser. The server receives the encrypted entry, the protected entry key, and only the metadata needed to store and retrieve the record.

visibility.title: What can the server actually see?
visibility.body: Encryption protects the contents of your journal, not every piece of metadata around it. The server still needs enough information to run the service, but that does not include plaintext journal content or usable journal-decryption keys.

observable.identity: Account identifiers such as your normalized username, display name, and opaque user ID.
observable.authentication: Key-schedule metadata, authentication-verifier material, and hashed session records.
observable.records: Entry IDs, creation and update times, ciphertext sizes, and record counts.
observable.operations: Request timing, IP-derived operational data, and access patterns.
observable.signIn: During account creation and sign-in, the derived authentication key used to verify your credentials.

private.derivedKeys: The password-derived master key or key-encryption key.

zeroKnowledge.title: What does zero knowledge mean here?
zeroKnowledge.body: In Blind Journal, zero knowledge means the server does not have the key material required to decrypt your journal. It can authenticate you, authorize requests, and store encrypted records without receiving plaintext journal content.
zeroKnowledge.limitsBody: It does not mean the server learns nothing about you. Account identifiers, record metadata, request timing, and access patterns remain observable. It also does not refer to mathematical zero-knowledge proof systems.
zeroKnowledge.browserBoundary: An unlocked journal is readable in your browser by design. Code already running in the same origin could potentially access that plaintext, so XSS prevention, dependency control, and a restrictive Content Security Policy are part of the security boundary.

architecture.title: How does the whole system fit together?
architecture.body: The browser owns the sensitive cryptographic work: it derives keys, encrypts outgoing journal content, and decrypts entries after they are returned. The API carries authentication and session data plus protected journal records across the network.
architecture.serverBody: The server validates and authorizes requests, manages sessions, and stores encrypted envelopes and observable metadata in the database. HTTPS protects the connection in transit; client-side encryption is what keeps journal content unreadable to the server itself.

technicalDepth.title: Built from established cryptographic primitives
technicalDepth.derivation: Blind Journal derives a short-lived 256-bit master key with Argon2id, then uses HKDF-SHA-256 with domain separation to derive independent authentication and AES-KW key-encryption material.
technicalDepth.entries: Each journal entry gets a random 256-bit AES-GCM key and a fresh 96-bit IV. The entry key is wrapped before storage, and authenticated additional data binds the encrypted envelope to its protocol version, user, and entry.
technicalDepth.implementation: Cryptographic operations use libsodium and the Web Crypto API rather than custom algorithms. The protocol is versioned so parameters can evolve without guessing how existing records were produced.

closing.title: Explore the implementation
closing.body: Blind Journal is open source. Review the implementation, protocol details, and security assumptions in the repository.

figures.bigPictureAlt: A readable journal and key remain in the browser, the journal is encrypted locally, and encrypted data is stored on the server.

figures.savingAlt: A journal entry and its entry key are protected locally, producing an encrypted entry and a protected key before the server stores them.
